hero.intro: Agentware is a class of software designed for the agentic era. You entrust it with a goal; within authorized bounds it organizes actions, executes tasks, and delivers verifiable outcomes.

questions.who: For the past forty years, software only asked you one question:
Now, software is beginning to answer a different question:

title: In the past, humans operated software
Now, humans delegate to software
intro: For decades, software was built around Features. Software provided buttons and forms, while humans acted as the sole dispatch center—you had to know which app to open, which button to click, which form to fill out, and in what order. Software offered fragmented capabilities; humans were responsible for stringing those capabilities together into outcomes.
Agents have transformed this relationship and rewritten the division-of-labor contract between humans and machines:

eras.body: Paths are hard-coded in advance. Humans click step by step; software passively responds.
AI accelerates single-point tasks (writing, drawing, coding), but humans still have to stitch every step together.
Humans entrust goals and constraints; software understands the task, plans autonomously, executes actions, observes feedback, and adapts dynamically until the outcome is delivered.

closing: This shift is not about bolting AI onto every piece of software—
it is about rewriting software itself.

notAgentware.title: Adding AI does not make it Agentware
notAgentware.lead: The difference lies not in whether a large language model is called, nor in whether there is a chat window, but in how the software operates beneath the surface.

items.name: AI Feature
items.body: Summarization, translation, search, and autocomplete are merely AI features inside traditional software. Efficiency improves, but the work is still operated and completed by humans.

items.name: Chatbot Wrapper
items.body: Adding a chat sidebar to legacy software, or wrapping a thin shell around a model API, still leaves old software underneath waiting for humans to click step by step.

items.name: Rigid Workflow
items.body: Fixed A → B → C → D pipelines are traditional automation. A workflow that freezes the moment reality deviates from presets lacks the ability to adapt to context and feedback.

items.name: Ungoverned Agent
items.body: Wild agents that loop blindly inside a black box with runaway costs and unverifiable outputs are experimental toys—not production-ready software.

architecture.body: Agentware does not replace deterministic code; it takes over the highest-level control logic. Beneath the surface remain rigorous databases, APIs, and business rules; at the top, "pre-written operation paths" give way to "organizing actions around goals at runtime."

loop.title: Paths are generated at runtime; outcomes are verified before delivery
principle: Goals can be delegated, and paths can be adaptive;
permissions must be explicit, outcomes must be verifiable, and processes must be governable.

steps.text: Make clear what outcome is wanted, within what boundaries to act, and what counts as done.
Gather the facts and experience relevant to the goal from the current environment and accumulated memory.
Organize actions around the goal and the current state, generating the execution path at runtime.
Within explicit authorization, call APIs, MCP, browsers and databases so actions take effect in real systems.
Read the results and changes an action produces, and check the actual state against what was expected.
Revise the plan with new information. When permission or risk boundaries are reached, return the decision to a human.
Check the result against the acceptance criteria defined in the delegation, keeping traceable evidence.
Deliver a verifiable outcome; if the goal cannot be met within scope, explain clearly and hand back to a human.

handback.text: Out of bounds: the system stops acting, explains why and what it has completed, and returns the decision to a human.

pillars.lead: For software to truly accept delegations, it must be built upon four foundational pillars:

items.lead: The fundamental unit of software shifts from features to delegations.
items.body: Traditional software starts by asking "what feature to build"; Agentware starts by asking "what outcome to entrust to the system." A clear delegation defines just four things: what outcome is desired, within what boundaries to act, what qualifies as acceptance, and when to hand control back to a human.

items.lead: Not just giving answers, but getting the job done.
items.body: Humans are no longer required to script every step in advance. The system determines the next move based on the goal and current state, acts upon the real world through real tools (APIs, MCP, CLI, browsers, databases, software systems), and advances through a closed loop of Plan → Act → Observe → Adapt.

items.lead: The greater the autonomy, the more vital the governance.
items.body: Agentware is not an unconstrained autonomous agent, but software equipped with execution power inside explicit authorization boundaries. Governance is just as critical as execution—every delegation must make clear: what it is permitted to do, what it actually did, how much cost it incurred, who can halt it at any moment, and how to roll back safely when errors occur.

items.lead: Memory transforms software from a one-off tool into a continuously evolving system.
items.body: Software without memory starts from zero every time; traditional retrieval (RAG) is merely passive document lookup. Agentware's memory system does more than answer questions—it directly participates in planning, decision-making, and action:
points: Preserves both the full context of specific tasks (episodic memory) and abstracted cognitive rules (semantic memory).
Breaks knowledge down into minimal intelligible units, automatically deduplicating, merging, revising, and distilling as new information arrives.
Every distilled memory can be traced back to its original source—auditable and trustworthy.

manifesto.intro: Software used to be a tool waiting to be operated. It provided functions; humans had to learn it, orchestrate it, and take responsibility for the results. Now, for the first time, software can be delegated work. This is not about bolting AI onto legacy software—it is about redefining what software should be in the age of agents.
items: I
Software should understand intent, not just input
In the past, humans had to translate their goals into a sequence of clicks and forms. Now, humans state what they want and what they won't accept—and software is responsible for understanding.
II
Software should execute goals, not just expose functions
No matter how many features exist, humans still had to string them together into outcomes. The value of software lies not in how many functions it exposes, but in what outcomes it delivers.
III
Paths may adapt
Outcomes must remain verifiable
Reality rarely unfolds according to preset workflows; execution paths must adapt to environment and feedback. The freer the path, the clearer the goal and acceptance criteria must be.
IV
Autonomy requires governance
We do not pursue unbounded autonomy. Every delegation must have explicit accountability and an auditable trail, always preserving human authority to intervene, roll back, and take over.
V
Memory turns software from a tool into an evolving system

A one-off executor starts from scratch every single time. Software that remembers context, accumulates experience, and refines itself grows to understand its people and organization better with every use.
VI
The future unit of software is not the feature
It is the delegation

In the past, designing software meant asking, "What feature goes here?" Today, designing software means asking, "What outcome should be entrusted to it?" Define the goal, boundaries, and acceptance criteria—and let the system complete the rest.

studio.sub: Agentware Studio is an independent research and creation studio dedicated to the Agentware paradigm. At the inflection point where software shifts from "operating interfaces" to "delegating intent," we advance the adoption and evolution of this paradigm through deep research, open curriculum, and product experiments:

items.title: AI Courses & Labs
items.body: A good technical course should be a solid piece of work in its own right. Built by practicing engineers, pairing visual animations with interactive web labs and runnable templates.

items.title: User-Facing AI Tool Experiments
items.body: Ideas must ultimately be validated by products. At aikit.pro, we continuously design and ship user-facing AI tools and applications, exploring how "software that acts on intent" feels in everyday workflows.

learn.title: AI Courses & Labs
motto: Built by engineers. Crafted to last.
learn.lead: A good technical course should be a solid piece of work in its own right. Every course at Agentware Studio is written and built by practicing engineers—turning abstract mechanics into clear visual intuition, pinning every demo to real models and versions, and pairing every lesson with interactive web labs and runnable templates you can put to work right away.
learn.status: Course 01 "Graduating from AI Gacha" now streaming · More engineering courses in production

course.name: Graduating from AI Gacha
course.body: Does using AI still feel like pulling a slot machine? When a model gives you bad output, the problem is usually what you put on its desk. Across three seasons, this course takes you from how large language models actually work, to coding with AI in your editor, to turning a real workflow into a working system. Every episode comes with a hands-on web game and an AI assistant that answers strictly from course materials with exact citations.

seasons.specs: Free · 14 animated episodes (incl. trailer) · No coding required
seasons.body: Using a desk and a gacha machine, we visualize how large language models work under the hood: how they predict one token tile at a time, why long chats make them lose track, how to hand them reference books and tools, and when you can trust their output. Each episode takes 5–8 minutes and leaves you with one concrete habit you can use the same day.

Writing code has gotten cheap; judging whether that code is right has gotten harder. Using VS Code (GitHub Copilot) and Claude Code side by side, we cover what files the agent actually sees, how to write project instructions (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md), how to review a plan before touching code, and how to package recurring team workflows into reusable Skills and automated hooks.

seasons.specs: Pro · 17 hands-on builds · For business leads & engineers
seasons.body: Built around six real workflows at a mid-sized company—weekly report automation, customer email triage, policy Q&A, an internal MCP server, multi-agent research, and cross-company agent handoffs. Step by step, you will sketch the architecture, engineer the context, build with n8n, Dify, or code, and run red-team safety tests, pass-rate evaluations, and ROI checks to ship a system ready for sign-off.

ui.markAria: AGENTWARE mark: the brackets are the authorized boundary, the rising path an execution path that can adapt, the point an outcome that must be verifiable. Click or press Enter to replay; use the arrow keys to move the path.

stage.n1done: The result is stitched by hand
stage.n2ai: AI speeds up a single task
stage.n2done: Humans still stitch every step together
aria: 1.0 The Tool Era: a cursor opens four function windows one by one, and the human stitches the result together by hand.
2.0 The Copilot Era: two of the functions are accelerated by AI, but every prompt starts from the human and returns to the human, who still links every step.

3.0 The Delegation Era: the human hands over one intent; inside the authorized boundary the system plans a path, re-routes around a blocked step, verifies the result and delivers a verifiable outcome.

loop.aria: The execution loop: understand the delegation and gather context, then plan, act, observe and adapt inside the authorized boundary, verify the result and deliver it or hand it back to a human. Below sits the deterministic core: memory, database, APIs and business rules.
loop.hint: After a run, select any step in the diagram to read about it.

logs.intent: Delegation received: goal, boundaries and acceptance criteria set
logs.context: Reading the current environment and relevant memory
logs.adapt: Plan revised: switching to another path
logs.verifyOk: Checked against acceptance criteria: passed, evidence kept
logs.act2warn: Requested action is outside the boundary; not executed
logs.observe2warn: Feedback: goal cannot be met within scope
logs.verifyFail: Acceptance failed: a human decision is needed
logs.handback: Stopped; reported why and what was done; handed back
